guide.title: Period 1 (1491–1607): review guide
guide.intro: Before 1492, the Americas held hundreds of diverse societies. European arrival began a period of exchange, conquest, and new systems of labor and identity that reshaped three continents. This guide reviews those developments and the causation questions the period raises.

sections.title: Native American societies before contact
body: Native societies adapted to very different environments. The spread of maize cultivation northward from present-day Mexico supported larger, settled populations, irrigation systems, and social hierarchies, for example in the Southwest. Peoples of the Great Basin and Great Plains developed mobile ways of life suited to scarce water and wide grasslands. In the Northeast and the Mississippi River Valley, many societies combined farming with hunting and lived in permanent villages; in the Pacific Northwest and California, rich fishing and gathering supported large, settled communities.

Contextualizing Period 1 means seeing these societies as dynamic and varied, not as a single “Native” culture, and recognizing that the encounter with Europeans began in a world already full of trade, politics, and change.
points: Environment shaped economy and settlement patterns.
Maize spread was a key cause of settled, complex societies.
Diversity of Native societies is a frequent exam theme.

sections.title: Exploration, conquest, and the Columbian Exchange
body: European exploration was driven by the search for new routes to Asian trade, competition among monarchies, religious motives, and new maritime technology. Spanish conquests of the Aztec and Inca empires brought enormous wealth, especially silver from Mexico and Peru.

The Columbian Exchange moved plants, animals, and diseases between hemispheres. Smallpox and other diseases killed a large share of Native peoples, who lacked immunity; horses, cattle, and pigs transformed American landscapes and some Native ways of life; American crops such as maize and potatoes helped European populations grow; and American silver fed European economies and the shift toward capitalism.
points: Causation: disease, not only warfare, explains much of the Native population collapse.
Silver flows strengthened Spain and spurred European commerce.

sections.title: Labor, caste, and cultural interactions
body: The Spanish encomienda system gave colonists the right to extract labor and tribute from Native people. As Native populations fell, the Spanish and Portuguese increasingly turned to enslaved Africans. A caste system ranked people by perceived mixtures of European, Native, and African ancestry.

Europeans debated how to treat Native peoples: in the Valladolid debate (1550–1551), Bartolomé de Las Casas argued that Native people were fully human and should not be enslaved, while Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda defended conquest. Native peoples and Africans resisted, adapted, and kept their own cultural practices even under pressure to convert.
points: Encomienda → enslaved African labor is a key change over time.
The caste system reflects European ideas about racial hierarchy.
Cultural interaction ran in many directions, including resistance.

example.prompt: Explain one cause of the decline of Native populations after 1492.
example.solution: European diseases such as smallpox spread rapidly among Native peoples who had no prior exposure or immunity, causing epidemics that killed large shares of many communities, often before Europeans even arrived in person.

misconceptions: “Native Americans lived in one kind of society.”
Societies varied greatly with their environments, from mobile groups to large settled farming communities.
Disease, Native alliances against the Aztecs, and division within empires mattered greatly.
“The Columbian Exchange only affected the Americas.”
It transformed Europe, Africa, and Asia too, through crops, silver, and the slave trade.
“Europeans all agreed about how to treat Native peoples.”
Some, like Las Casas, strongly criticized Spanish treatment.

passages.title: Source A: Christopher Columbus, letter describing his first voyage, 1493
text: “This island, like all the others, is most extensive. It has many ports along the sea-coast excelling any in Christendom—and many fine, large, flowing rivers. . . . Hispaniola is a marvel. Its hills and mountains, fine plains and open country, are rich and fertile for planting and for pasturage, and for building towns and villages. The seaports there are incredibly fine, as also the magnificent rivers, most of which bear gold. . . . There are many spices and vast mines of gold and other metals in this island. They have no iron, nor steel, nor weapons, nor are they fit for them, because although they are well-made men of commanding stature, they appear extraordinarily timid.”
passages.attribution: Christopher Columbus, letter to Luis de Santángel, an official of the Spanish court who had helped finance the voyage, 1493 (English translation). Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 2.1.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/2-1-portuguese-exploration-and-spanish-conquest); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Two interpretations of the Columbian Exchange
text: Interpretation 1: “The most important consequence of 1492 was biological. Within a few generations, epidemics of smallpox, measles, and other diseases had killed a majority of the Native population in many regions. Without this catastrophe, Spanish conquest would have been far slower and far less complete.”

Interpretation 2: “Disease alone does not explain the transformation of the Americas. Spanish conquest depended on alliances with Native peoples who resented Aztec rule, and colonial labor systems that forced survivors into mines and fields deepened the decline. Human choices, not only microbes, shaped the outcome.”

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of Native American societies before 1492
text: “Long before Europeans arrived, the peoples of North America had built societies as varied as the land itself. Where maize could be grown and water managed, as in the Southwest, people built multistory towns and complex irrigation systems. On the Great Plains and in the Great Basin, where rainfall was scarce, many groups moved with the seasons to hunt and gather. In the Northeast, villages surrounded by cornfields stood near forests where men hunted. These were not unchanging societies waiting to be discovered; they traded, fought, migrated, and adapted for centuries.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of Spanish colonial society
text: “Spanish America was organized around labor and lineage. Through the encomienda, Spanish settlers claimed the work and tribute of Native communities, and as those communities shrank, colonists imported growing numbers of enslaved Africans. Colonial authorities sorted the resulting population into a ladder of categories based on European, Native, and African ancestry, with peninsulares, people born in Spain, at the top. Yet the system was never complete: Native and African peoples preserved languages and beliefs, blended them with Catholic practices, and sometimes rose in revolt.”

questions.prompt: Columbus most likely emphasized the islands' gold, spices, and harbors in order to
choices: describe Native religious beliefs in detail
encourage continued Spanish financial support for further voyages
warn other Europeans not to settle the islands
argue that the islands should remain uncolonized
questions.explanation: Writing to a court official who had helped fund the voyage, Columbus highlighted wealth that would justify more expeditions.
choiceExplanations: The excerpt says nothing about Native religion.
He praises the islands rather than warning anyone away.
His descriptions of towns and pasturage point toward colonization.

military rivals equal to Spain
people who could be easily dominated
traders who would control the gold supply
questions.explanation: Noting they have “no iron, nor steel, nor weapons” and are “extraordinarily timid” presents them as vulnerable.
choiceExplanations: He says they have no iron or steel.
He describes them as lacking weapons.
He doesn't describe them as traders.

questions.prompt: Reports like the one in the excerpt most directly contributed to which development in the following decades?
choices: An alliance between Spain and the Aztec Empire
The founding of English colonies in New England
Spanish expeditions and conquests in search of gold and silver in the Americas
The end of European interest in trade with Asia
questions.explanation: Promises of wealth helped drive Spanish conquest, from the Caribbean to the Aztec and Inca empires.
choiceExplanations: Spain conquered the Aztec Empire rather than allying with it.
English New England colonies came over a century later, for different reasons.
Europeans continued to seek Asian trade.

questions.prompt: A historian might question how fully the excerpt describes Native societies on Hispaniola mainly because
choices: Columbus never visited Hispaniola
the letter was written centuries after the voyage
Columbus was a member of the Taíno people
Columbus had a motive to stress wealth and Native weakness, and little understanding of Taíno society
questions.explanation: The letter's purpose and its author's limited knowledge shape what it includes, so it is a partial view of Native life.
choiceExplanations: The letter describes his own voyage to the island.
It was written in 1493, right after the voyage.
Columbus was a European explorer sailing for Spain.

choices: Climate change in the 1600s
Epidemic diseases brought by Europeans
Migration of Native peoples to Europe
Wars among Native nations before 1492
questions.explanation: It argues that disease was the most important consequence and cause of the rapid decline.
choiceExplanations: Climate isn't mentioned.
This didn't happen on any significant scale.
It discusses effects after 1492, not earlier wars.

questions.prompt: Interpretation 2 differs from Interpretation 1 mainly in arguing that
choices: the Columbian Exchange began in the 1700s
Spain never conquered the Aztec Empire
disease had no effect on Native populations
Native alliances and Spanish labor systems also shaped the outcome, not disease alone
questions.explanation: Interpretation 2 accepts disease as part of the story but stresses human choices and labor systems.
choiceExplanations: Neither interpretation dates it that way.
It describes the conquest's dependence on alliances.
It says disease alone doesn't explain the outcome, not that it had no effect.

questions.prompt: Which piece of evidence would best support Interpretation 2?
choices: Spanish forces under Cortés fought alongside thousands of Tlaxcalan allies against the Aztecs
Europeans had no immunity to American diseases
Smallpox reached the Aztec capital in 1520
Horses were unknown in the Americas before 1492
questions.explanation: Native allies' role in the conquest supports the claim that human alliances, not only disease, shaped the outcome.
choiceExplanations: This is inaccurate and irrelevant: the epidemics struck Native peoples.
This supports Interpretation 1's emphasis on disease.
This concerns the exchange of animals, not the cause of decline.

questions.prompt: Both interpretations would most likely agree that the Columbian Exchange
choices: was mainly an exchange of ideas rather than goods and organisms
had devastating consequences for Native peoples of the Americas
had little effect on the population of the Americas
benefited Native and European peoples equally
questions.explanation: Both describe a sharp decline in Native populations; they disagree about its causes.
choiceExplanations: Both focus on disease and labor, which are biological and material.
Both describe dramatic population effects.
Neither suggests equal benefits.

They were isolated and did not trade
They developed different ways of life adapted to their environments
They all depended on large-scale maize agriculture
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts Southwest towns, mobile Plains and Great Basin groups, and Northeast villages.
choiceExplanations: It describes multistory towns and villages.
The passage says they traded.
Plains and Great Basin groups often relied on hunting and gathering.

choices: The spread of horses introduced by the Spanish
The growth of tobacco plantations
The building of irrigation canals
The founding of French fur-trading posts in the Southwest
questions.explanation: Horses, part of the Columbian Exchange, transformed hunting, travel, and warfare on the Plains.
choiceExplanations: Tobacco plantations developed in the Chesapeake.
Irrigation was a Southwest practice, not a Plains change.

questions.prompt: The interpretation's final sentence is best understood as a response to which view?
choices: That trade began only after 1492
That Native societies were static and unchanged before Europeans arrived
That Europeans brought maize to the Americas
That Native societies were all nomadic
questions.explanation: By stressing that Native peoples traded, fought, migrated, and adapted, the author rejects the idea of unchanging societies.
choiceExplanations: It mentions trade, but the sentence's target is the idea of static societies.
Maize was domesticated in the Americas; the passage doesn't address that claim.
The passage already showed variety earlier; the final sentence addresses change over time.
